title: Page-aware predictive eviction probe log
content:
Summary

This note captures the exploratory run where we injected a lightweight page-awareness signal into the eviction ranking for the KV cache and evaluated effects on reuse rates, tail latency, page faults, and DRAM bandwidth under mixed inference workloads. The overall goal was to see whether small, local heuristics that penalize items likely to trigger cold page faults reduce long-tail latency without materially hurting overall reuse/hit-rate.

Motivation & hypothesis

Observed problem: under multi-tenant traces with heterogeneous sequence lengths, eviction choices sometimes evict entries that move onto a different NUMA node page boundary and cause expensive cross-node page faults or DRAM surge when reloaded. This shows up as sporadic 95/99 p95+p99 latency spikes even when nominal hit-rate is high.

Hypothesis: adding a low-cost predictive penalty to eviction score that prefers keeping entries with high recent intra-page reuse (and penalizes entries that have coldness combined with page transitions) will reduce page-fault-driven tail events and smooth memory bandwidth spikes. The penalty must be tunable to avoid degrading aggregate hit-rate.

Design of the probe

- Eviction scoring baseline: LRU-ish recency score + reuse_count_weighted.
- New signals appended: page_hotness_score (0..1 float) computed from a 1KB-aligned page reuse counter, and page_transition_flag (binary) if entry was updated/used from a different physical page recently.
- Combined eviction_score = base_score + alpha * (1 - page_hotness_score) + beta * page_transition_flag.
- We experimented with alpha in {0.25, 0.5, 1.0} and beta in {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}.
- TTL fallback: entries with explicit TTL remain protected until TTL expiry; the probe only affects eviction ordering for non-TTL entries.

Implementation notes

- Page counters implemented as a per-GPU (per-process) small dense table keyed by page-aligned KV slot pointer (8-bit saturating counters). Counters increment on slot hits; decay via periodic right-shift every 10s to keep hotness responsive.
- page_transition_flag toggled when a slot's physical page address differs from the previous access’s page address (sampled on each lookup). We tracked transitions with a 16-bit last-page-id per slot.
- Memory overhead: new per-slot counters added 1 byte + 2 bytes = 3 bytes per slot (we aligned to 4 bytes). For a 128M-entry cache this is ~512MB additional residency — unacceptable for large configs; for the probe we limited to a 16M-entry working set region using address hashing.

Workloads and bench harness

We used three representative traces:
- trace-A (real): small-seq chat workload (median seq=64, tail seq=512). Multi-tenant mix with 10% heavy embeddings calls.
- trace-B (synthetic): long-seq document summarization (median seq=1024, tails to 2k), with highly correlated prefixes.
- trace-C (mixed): 50/50 mix of small chat + long-batch; includes bursty fanout patterns that exercise prefetch & eviction.

Each trace ran across 8 GPUs in our staging cluster, capped to same QPS baseline (to make memory bandwidth comparable). We ran each configuration for 45 minutes steady-state after a warmup of 10 minutes.

Telemetry & profiling

Collected signals: per-token latency histogram (p50/p95/p99), eviction rate, reuse-rate (per-slot), page-fault rate (soft+hard), DRAM read bandwidth from perf counters, GPU stall time attributable to memory (NVTX regions around KV loads), and OS-level page reclaim metrics.

We used: perf (kernel PMUs), nvprof sampling for GPU kernel/memory hotspots, eBPF tracepoints for page-faults, and a lightweight in-runtime profiler that recorded slot lookup times and page-id transitions to a circular buffer (sampled 0.1%).

Key results (high-level)

- alpha=0.5, beta=1.0 was the best compromise for trace-C (mixed). This setting reduced p99 latency by ~12% relative to baseline while decreasing page-fault events by ~28%. Aggregate hit-rate dropped by 0.6 percentage points (from 89.7% to 89.1%).
- For trace-B (long sequences) the predictive penalty caused small hit-rate regressions (1.2 pp) and negligible latency gains; likely because long sequences naturally thrash page boundaries less (larger contiguous loads).
- For trace-A (small chat) there were modest gains in 95/99 with no measurable hit-rate loss.

Detailed numbers (sampled averages over steady-state window)

trace-C (mixed), baseline vs best probe (alpha=0.5,beta=1.0):
- p50: 6.8 ms -> 6.6 ms
- p95: 28.2 ms -> 26.4 ms
- p99: 132.6 ms -> 116.7 ms
- hit-rate: 89.7% -> 89.1%
- eviction-rate: 11.2k evictions/s -> 10.8k evictions/s
- page-faults (soft+hard): 420 /min -> 305 /min
- observed DRAM read BW 95th pct: 120 GB/s -> 103 GB/s

Profiling anecdotes

- We observed several 200–300ms user-visible stalls coincident with the OS performing cross-node page migration. These stalls aligned with sequences that re-requested entries previously evicted and which lived on a different physical page.
- The per-slot last-page-id heuristic caught cases where hot KV slots had flip-flopped between two adjacent pages (a noisy allocator pattern) — protecting these reduced oscillatory evictions.
- The page-counter decay interval (10s default) is important: too slow and stale hotness keeps cold pages resident; too fast and short-lived hot edges are not distinguished. 10s was empirically balanced for our traces.

Costs and limitations

- Memory overhead: naive per-slot metadata is expensive. For production we need one of: sampled metadata (track only a subset of slots), bloom-filtered page-tags per region, or move counters to a compact hardware-assisted structure.
- Complexity: adding page-awareness increases bookkeeping on lookup path. Our optimized C path added ~2.2ns median per-lookup in microbench; small but accumulates at very high QPS.
- Platform dependence: behavior varies heavily across NUMA configs and allocator strategies. On instances with hugepages enabled and stable allocations the benefit shrinks.

Comparison vs other strategies

- Pure TTL-based approaches: TTL reduces churn but is coarse; page-aware probe adds selectivity by protecting hot pages rather than arbitrary TTL ranges.
- Prefetching strategies: prefetching reduces misses but can amplify bandwidth spikes if misapplied. Combining prefetch with page-aware scoring gave the best stability in trace-C (prefetch on kept entries only).

Open questions and follow-ups

1) Sampling strategy: can we maintain similar benefits by tracking only 10% of slots cheaply? Run a sample vs full metadata comparison.
2) Hardware offload: explore whether hardware page-tagging (or using existing TLB/perf hints) can supply page-hotness with negligible overhead.
3) TTL vs score gating: create an adaptive controller that increases alpha when page-fault rate exceeds threshold.
4) Edge cases: quantify effect on workloads with controlled allocator behavior (hugepages vs 4K pages).
5) Long-term stability: run 72-hour soak tests under production traces to ensure no slow regression patterns.

Immediate action items

- [Diego] land the sampling proxy PR that exposes sampled per-slot counters (GH:1423-sampling-proxy). Target: 2026-03-12.
- [Lena] run a 72-hr soak on staging-large with alpha=0.5,beta=1.0 + sampled metadata. Report memory footprint and p99 trends. Target: 2026-03-20.
- [Ravi] investigate allocator changes (enable/disable hugetlb) on a per-image basis and capture page-id flip frequency. Target: 2026-03-15.
- [Aisha] consolidate microbench numbers and iterate on decay interval tuning (5s, 10s, 20s).

Artifacts attached / references

- Quick perf snapshots and flamegraphs saved to: GH artifacts in PR redwood-inference/serving-runtime#1423 (look under builds/artifacts/page-aware-probe).
- Confluence design writeup: internal link in metadata.
- Raw sampled profiler buffers: archived in S3: s3://redwood-stage/profiles/page-aware-probe/traceC-run-20260304.tar.gz

Notes to reviewers

This is intentionally exploratory and has knobs that are likely overfit to our current staging allocator. Focus review on whether the scoring formula and decay semantics are reasonable, and whether the sampling strategies suggested are implementable without breaking existing invariants. We want a defensible incremental roll path (sampled metadata -> opt-in flag -> default on for dedicated capacity) rather than a big switch.

Appendix: quick microbench numbers (single-threaded lookup hot-path)

- baseline lookup median: 85 ns; mean: 97 ns
- with full page-metadata checks: median: 87.2 ns; mean: 101 ns
- with sampled metadata (10% checks): median: 85.6 ns; mean: 98 ns

End of probe log.
